hints: Think about what type of reactive species is formed from $\text{Cl}_2$ in sunlight and what happens to a hydrogen on propane.
walkthrough:
Link sunlight to radicals**
Sunlight provides energy to split $\text{Cl}_2$ into highly reactive $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ radicals. When an alkane reacts with chlorine this way, a hydrogen atom is replaced by a chlorine atom, so you are substituting.
Final answer: free-radical substitution

hints: Recall that propagation keeps radicals going, one radical in and one new radical out in each step.
Think about what $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ does to $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8$ first, then what the carbon radical does to $\text{Cl}_2$.
Remember termination joins two radicals together so no radicals remain, and here the product must be $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$.
walkthrough:
Build propagation 1**
A $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ radical is hungry for another electron. It abstracts a hydrogen from propane: $$\mathrm{C_3H_8 + Cl^{\bullet} \rightarrow C_3H_7^{\bullet} + HCl}$$ You make $\text{HCl}$ and a new carbon radical, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^\bullet$. A radical is consumed and a new one is formed, so the chain continues.

Build propagation 2**
Now the carbon radical attacks a $\text{Cl}_2$ molecule: $$\mathrm{C_3H_7^{\bullet} + Cl_2 \rightarrow C_3H_7Cl + Cl^{\bullet}}$$ You make the 1-chloropropane product and regenerate $\text{Cl}^\bullet$, which can go back to Step 1. That regeneration is the key idea of propagation.

Build the required termination**
Termination must remove radicals by combining them. To make the named product $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$, join the two radicals directly: $$\mathrm{C_3H_7^{\bullet} + Cl^{\bullet} \rightarrow C_3H_7Cl}$$ No dots remain on the right, so the chain stops. Remember to include the dot $^\bullet$ on every radical, otherwise you lose the mark.

Final answer: propagation 1: $\mathrm{C_3H_8 + Cl^{\bullet} \rightarrow C_3H_7^{\bullet} + HCl}$
propagation 2: $\mathrm{C_3H_7^{\bullet} + Cl_2 \rightarrow C_3H_7Cl + Cl^{\bullet}}$
termination: $\mathrm{C_3H_7^{\bullet} + Cl^{\bullet} \rightarrow C_3H_7Cl}$
Accept $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2^{\bullet}}$ for $\mathrm{C_3H_7^{\bullet}}$ and $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2Cl}$ for $\mathrm{C_3H_7Cl}$.

hints: Look at the initiation equation $\text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Cl}^\bullet$ and ask how the shared electron pair is split.
walkthrough:
See equal sharing**
In $\text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Cl}^\bullet$ each chlorine keeps one electron from the shared pair. One electron goes each way to give two radicals. That equal split is homolytic fission.
Final answer: homolytic (fission)

hints: Count the longest carbon chain and locate the two chlorine atoms on the displayed structure of Q.
walkthrough:
Number and name**
Q has three carbons in a row, so it is propane. One $\text{Cl}$ is on carbon 1 ($\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ end) and one $\text{Cl}$ is on carbon 2 (middle carbon). Number to give the lowest locants, so it is 1,2-dichloropropane.

hints: For structural isomerism, think about the different ways two Cl atoms can be placed on a three carbon skeleton.
For stereoisomerism, look for a carbon with four different groups attached in one of the $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{Cl}_2$ isomers.
walkthrough:
Spot positional isomerism**
With formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{Cl}_2$ you can have 1,1-, 1,2-, 1,3- and 2,2-dichloropropane. Only the positions of the $\text{Cl}$ atoms change while the carbon skeleton stays the same. That is positional isomerism.

Spot optical isomerism**
Look closely at 1,2-dichloropropane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CHClCH}_2\text{Cl}$. Carbon 2 is attached to $\text{H}$, $\text{Cl}$, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$, four different groups. It is a chiral centre, so the molecule exists as a pair of non-superimposable mirror images. That is optical isomerism.

Final answer: type of structural isomerism: positional
type of stereoisomerism: optical

hints: Reaction 2 converts $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, think which hydroxide source and solvent replaces Cl by OH.
walkthrough:
Choose hydrolysis conditions**
You need to swap $\text{Cl}$ for $\text{OH}$ by nucleophilic substitution. Warm with aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ provides $\text{OH}^-$ as nucleophile and water as solvent. Do not write ethanolic $\text{NaOH}$, that would give elimination to an alkene.
Final answer: sodium hydroxide AND water (aqueous sodium hydroxide)

hints: Recall the colour of acidified dichromate(VI) and the colour of the chromium(III) ion formed when it oxidises a primary alcohol.
walkthrough:
Remember the test**
Acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ is orange $\text{Cr(VI)}$. As it oxidises propan-1-ol, it is itself reduced to $\text{Cr}^{3+}$, which is green. So you see orange to green.

hints: Reaction 3 oxidises $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ fully to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ under reflux, count how many [O] atoms are needed to balance.
walkthrough:
Balance with [O]**
Heating under reflux with excess oxidant takes a primary alcohol all the way to the carboxylic acid. Add two atoms of oxygen from the oxidant: $$\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH + 2[O] \rightarrow CH_3CH_2COOH + H_2O}$$ Check atoms: both sides have $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}_3$, so it balances.

hints: Carboxylic acid plus alcohol gives ester plus water, think what name describes joining two molecules with loss of a small molecule.
walkthrough:
Name the joining**
$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH} + \text{R-OH} \rightarrow \text{ester S} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. Two molecules join and water is eliminated. That is a condensation reaction, specifically esterification.
Final answer: condensation (esterification)

hints: Use Table 4.2 to match the strong peak near $1750 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ to a carbonyl bond found in esters.
Look for a peak in the $1500$ to $1680 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ region that proves the alcohol R was unsaturated.
Find the strong absorption in the $1040$ to $1300 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ fingerprint region that confirms the ester linkage.
walkthrough:
Prove the ester carbonyl**
The very strong, sharp dip at about $1750 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ falls in the $1710$ to $1750 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ range for an ester $\text{C=O}$. Label this on Fig. 4.2. This confirms the $\text{C=O}$ part of the ester.

Prove unsaturation**
The absorption at about $1650 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ falls in the $1500$ to $1680 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ range for $\text{C=C}$. Label this. It shows S still contains an alkene bond from unsaturated alcohol R.

Prove the ester C-O**
The strong absorption at about $1170 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ falls in the $1040$ to $1300 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ range for $\text{C-O}$ in an ester. Label this. Together, $\text{C=O}$ plus $\text{C-O}$ confirms an ester, and $\text{C=C}$ confirms unsaturation.

Final answer: absorption 1 at approx. $\mathrm{1750\ cm^{-1}}$: $\mathrm{C=O}$
absorption 2 at approx. $\mathrm{1650\ cm^{-1}}$: $\mathrm{C=C}$
absorption 3 at approx. $\mathrm{1170\ cm^{-1}}$: $\mathrm{C-O}$

hints: Recall that the height of the [M+1] peak relative to M+ comes mainly from $^{13}\text{C}$, about 1.1% per carbon atom.
walkthrough:
Apply the 1.1% rule**
Each carbon contributes about 1.1% to the $\text{[M+1]}^+$ peak. So: $$\text{number of C} = \frac{\text{abundance of [M+1]}^+}{\text{abundance of M}^+} \times \frac{100}{1.1}$$ $$= \frac{0.31}{4.7} \times \frac{100}{1.1} = 5.996 \approx 6$$ So S contains 6 carbon atoms.
Final answer: number of carbon atoms in S = 6
